On February 28th, a vulnerability was discovered in the contract of Seneca, an omnichain CDP protocol on the Ethereum network. Hackers exploited constructed calldata parameters to call transferfrom, transferring tokens authorized to the project contract to their address, ultimately exchanging them for ETH. Seneca was exploited by hackers for over 1900 ETH, valued at approximately $6.5 million. On February 29th, the hacker address of SenecaUSD returned 1537 ETH (approximately $5.3 million) to the deployer address of Seneca.

On February 28, 2024, Seneca Protocol suffered an exploit on Ethereum and Arbitrum. Attackers abused a Chamber contract's arbitrary external call capability, enabling unauthorized ERC20 transfers from user wallets and draining over $6.4M. Most funds were later returned following negotiations. The Chamber contract allowed arbitrary external calls via performOperations, letting attackers execute token transfers from any address the contract had approval for without verification.

A bug in Seneca Protocol's smart contract has allowed attackers to steal funds from users who had approved the contract. So far, around $3 million has been stolen across the Ethereum blockchain and Arbitrum layer-2 . Making things worse, although the project's smart contract inherits the Pausable module that should allow the Seneca team to halt the malfunctioning code, they never implemented the function, meaning there's no way for them to stop the thefts. Instead, individual users must each revoke access to the flawed contract.
